idiom_name: handler object with one function per node type, driven by the traversal framework
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no method overloading, so the GoF structure degenerates: the visitor is a plain object whose keys are node types (or type aliases) and whose values are functions, and the traversal framework - not an accept() method - calls handler(node, state) for every node it reaches. Babel plugins work exactly this way (visitor: { Identifier(path) {} }, plus enter/exit phases, alias expansion and per-node-type dispatch through VISITOR_KEYS) and ESLint rules return a handler map from create(context). The first dispatch is therefore a data lookup instead of a virtual call, and operations stay first-class values that can be merged, ordered and even serialised. Write the classic accept()/visit() class form only when elements are classes with behaviour of their own - there is no compile-time coverage to gain in JavaScript, so the handler map is usually both smaller and more flexible.
pitfalls: Handlers are selected by the node's type string, so a typo or a renamed node type never fires; frameworks that validate visitor keys (Babel throws for unknown types) catch this, ad-hoc traversers do not.
instanceof is unreliable as a dispatch key across realms, iframes and transpiled classes; switch on an explicit type/kind field instead.
State stored on the visitor object is shared between concurrent traversals and between nested visitors - pass state as the second argument rather than mutating the visitor.
Creating a fresh visitor object inside a hot visitor (a nested traverse per node) defeats framework caches that mark visitors as already normalised; hoist the object.

variants.name: Class-based accept() / visit() double dispatch
variants.idiom_name: Element classes with accept(visitor) and a Visitor class per operation
variants.implementation_notes: The literal GoF translation to JavaScript classes: every element class implements accept(visitor) by calling the method named for its own type, and a visitor class implements one method per element type (or a single visit(node) plus type checks). It earns its place when the elements genuinely are classes with behaviour, when the operation must be an object carrying configuration that is passed around and injected (the classic testing benefit), or when interop requires the shape. The traversal must be written explicitly - nothing calls the visitor for you - and because JavaScript has no compile-time completeness check, a new element class does not break existing visitors; the missing case surfaces at run time instead.
pitfalls: A subclass that forgets to override accept() inherits the base implementation and dispatches the wrong visit method; with no compiler check, test each element type against each visitor.
Method names are the dispatch table: a typo (visitCirle) is a run-time TypeError, so keep the names in one place or validate handlers at construction.
Objects deserialised from JSON lose their prototype, so instanceof-based dispatch and accept() both break on data that came back from a wire or a cache.

Because JavaScript has no compile-time completeness check, adding an element class does not break existing visitors - the missing case surfaces at run time, the opposite of the tradeoff in statically typed languages.
